issues.legal_issue: The right of private defence ends when the threat to the person or property has ceased, and force used after that point is not protected by that right.
material_facts: The accused and their companions initially faced an armed crowd threatening their possession of the field, and the court accepted that they initially had a right of private defence.
After a firearm was first used and a villager was killed, the crowd fled and the immediate danger to the accused and their property had ended.
The accused then fired at two victims who were at considerable distances from them.
issues.conclusion: The accused could not claim the protection of private defence for the later killings, and their convictions for murder were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 99 and 100 of the Indian Penal Code, force in private defence must not be disproportionate to the injury to be averted and must remain within its legitimate purpose. Under sections 102 and 105, the right continues only while the danger or reasonable apprehension persists; force must stop when the threat disappears. The right is not vindictive or malicious, although the court may account for the excitement and confusion of a person facing an assault and should not assess the force with detached hindsight. The judgment also refers to Mayne's Criminal Law of India on not requiring a threatened person to modulate a defence blow by blow while an attack continues.

rule.if: murder_appeal_with_private_defence_claim and initial_threat_to_person_or_property and threat_ended_before_fatal_force and fatal_force_used_after_threat_ended

predicates.murder_appeal_with_private_defence_claim: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a murder conviction in which the accused claims private defence.
predicates.initial_threat_to_person_or_property: The accused initially faced a real and immediate threat to a person or property.
predicates.threat_ended_before_fatal_force: The threat to the person or property had ended before the fatal force was used.
predicates.fatal_force_used_after_threat_ended: The accused used fatal force after the threat had ended.

issues.definition: When a murder appeal involves an initial threat and fatal force used only after that threat ended, the rule denies private-defence protection for that later force.

issues.legal_issue: An omission to put a particular evidentiary circumstance to an accused does not by itself invalidate the trial if the examination as a whole gave a fair opportunity to explain the prosecution case and the omission caused no prejudice.
material_facts: The trial judge did not specifically put to one accused the distance between him and the victim when the shot was fired.
The remaining questions gave the accused an opportunity to address the prosecution case, and the court considered the omitted point immaterial to the conclusion that the threat had ceased.
The accused argued that the omission vitiated the trial.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not vitiate the trial or affect the appellate conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the court to put relevant circumstances appearing in the evidence to the accused so that the accused can explain them, but does not require detailed questioning amounting to cross-examination. The ultimate test is whether the accused had an opportunity, considering all questions put, to say what they wished about the prosecution case; a defect causing prejudice is a serious infirmity. The court applied Hate Singh Bhagat Singh v. State of Madhya Bharat and held that it did not impose an inexorable rule that every omitted point invalidates a trial or conviction.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_after_conviction and accused_examination_omitted_specific_circumstance and examination_as_a_whole_allowed_response and omission_caused_no_prejudice

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal following a conviction.
predicates.accused_examination_omitted_specific_cir: The court did not specifically put one evidentiary circumstance to the accused during questioning.
predicates.examination_as_a_whole_allowed_response: Considering all questions asked, the accused had a fair opportunity to respond to the prosecution case.
predicates.omission_caused_no_prejudice: The omitted circumstance did not cause prejudice to the accused.

issues.definition: If questioning omitted a specific circumstance but otherwise allowed a fair response and caused no prejudice, the omission does not invalidate the trial or conviction.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of ballistic expert evidence does not undermine proof of a shooting when the alleged firearms were not recovered and the recovered firearm was not alleged by the prosecution to have caused the deaths.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused used rifles, but those rifles were not recovered.
A revolver was recovered, but its connection to the shootings formed part of the defence account, not the prosecution's case.
The accused argued that the prosecution should have called a ballistic expert.
issues.conclusion: The absence of ballistic expert evidence did not undermine the prosecution case, and Mohinder Singh v. The State did not apply to these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment distinguished Mohinder Singh v. The State, which discusses the prosecution's duty to establish by expert evidence that injuries could have been caused by the alleged weapon and in the alleged manner. Here the alleged rifles were unavailable for examination, and the prosecution did not claim that the recovered revolver caused the deaths, so expert evidence about that revolver was not required to prove the prosecution's case.

predicates.appeal_challenging_murder_proof: The proceeding is an appeal challenging proof of a murder charge.
predicates.prosecution_alleges_firearm_killings: The prosecution alleges that the deaths were caused by firearms used by the accused.
predicates.alleged_firearms_unavailable_for_examina: The firearms alleged by the prosecution were not available for expert examination.
predicates.recovered_firearm_not_prosecution_allege: Any recovered firearm was not alleged by the prosecution to be the weapon that caused the deaths.

issues.definition: When a murder appeal challenges firearm proof, the alleged firearms are unavailable, and a recovered firearm is not the prosecution's alleged weapon, lack of ballistic expert evidence does not undermine the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reach a different assessment of prosecution witnesses from the trial court when it reconsiders the evidence, particularly where the disagreement is not based on witness demeanour.
material_facts: The trial court rejected some evidence concerning certain accused but accepted the major part of the prosecution evidence about the occurrence.
The appellate court considered individual cases after rejecting the trial court's reliance on joint liability and reached different conclusions about the accused.
The criticism of the witnesses related mainly to their partisan character and overstatements, rather than their demeanour.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was entitled to reconsider the evidence and its findings about the victims and the accused were not invalid merely because they differed from the trial court's assessment.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court is normally reluctant to differ from a trial court's assessment of oral evidence because the trial court can observe witnesses' demeanour, but it may do so in a proper case after reconsidering the evidence. The court noted that the trial court had substantially believed the prosecution account of the occurrence and that the disputed criticism was not principally about demeanour.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction.
predicates.appellate_court_reassesses_witness_evide: The appellate court independently reconsiders the witness evidence.
predicates.trial_court_assessment_not_based_on_deme: The trial court's disputed assessment was not principally based on observing witness demeanour.

issues.definition: When an appellate court reconsiders witness evidence and the trial court's disputed assessment was not principally based on demeanour, the appellate court may reach a different view.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence may be reduced when the circumstances of the offence, including continuing excitement after a threat has ended, provide an extenuating basis for a lesser sentence.
material_facts: The accused were convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

The court held that the threat had ended before the accused fired the fatal shots, but considered the background of the incident, the threat posed by the crowd, and the excitement that may have continued in the accused's minds.
The State did not press for the death sentence.
issues.conclusion: The death sentences were set aside and replaced with sentences of imprisonment for life, while the murder convictions were confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing sentence, the court considered the background of the incident, the nature and extent of the threat, and the excitement that may have persisted even after the right of private defence had ended; in the special circumstances, that excitement was an extenuating circumstance warranting a lesser sentence.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction_with_death: The proceeding is an appeal from a murder conviction carrying a death sentence.
predicates.threat_had_ended_before_killing: The threat had ended before the accused committed the killing.
predicates.continuing_excitement_and_incident_conte: The circumstances of the incident support finding that excitement persisted and is extenuating.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a murder conviction with a death sentence and the context supports an extenuating finding of continuing excitement after the threat ended, the death sentence is reduced to a lesser sentence.
